task: For each item report A, B, insufficient, or both_or_conflicting. Treat the alternatives symmetrically. Do not fill gaps by plausibility, clinical expectation, or what an interviewer may wish to elicit. Keep negation, uncertainty, time and whose experience is described intact. Use insufficient when neither specific alternative is established, and both_or_conflicting only when specific evidence actually supports both. For A/B give evidence for that alternative; for both_or_conflicting give evidence for each alternative, tagging each citation supports=A or supports=B. Quote short exact contiguous substrings and 1-based turn numbers. Provide a short reasoning sentence for each item. Return one JSON object keyed by the two supplied item identifiers. Each value has choice, reason and citations. Each citation has turn (integer), role (patient or interviewer), quote (exact text) and supports (A or B). Use an empty citations array when insufficient.
evidence_rule: Use the patient's own words as evidence. The interviewer's statements alone do not establish the patient's answer. If relying on an elliptical yes/no or a similar short agreement/disagreement, quote both the exact patient reply and the question it answers from the same numbered turn, tagged with the same alternative. Explain the link. Retain ambiguity if the patient does not endorse the premise.

interview.interviewer: What has occupied most of your attention this past week?
interview.patient:
Mostly getting the reading done for my geography class. I like the course, but I want to stop leaving the reading until the trip there. I used a slip of paper under the line last week, and that helped me finish a short passage.

And I straightened a bent mudguard on my sibling’s bike last weekend. I get quite absorbed in that—if I lose track, I can look at the wheel and see where I was. With reading, it’s harder to find my way back.

interview.interviewer: Can you give me an example of something you worked on with your hands recently?
interview.patient: "The mudguard I mentioned on my sibling’s bike—that was last weekend. It was bent and rubbing against the wheel, so I straightened it. I like that sort of thing because… well, you can see where it’s catching. If I get distracted, I can look at it again and pick up where I left off."

interview.interviewer: How does a practical task compare with doing some reading?
interview.patient: With the bike, I can see what I’ve done and what still needs fixing. Reading… I can be looking at the line but lose how it connects to the bit before, so I have to go back. Especially if people are talking nearby. It’s easier in the library, where it’s quiet.

interview.interviewer: Can you pick it up again easily?
interview.patient: "With reading, not so easily. I can find the line, but… I have to go back a bit to get the sense of it again. With the bike, I can usually see where I left off."

interview.interviewer: I meant a piece of reading. If you lose your place, how do you get going again?
interview.patient: I go back a few lines and read them again until it makes sense, then carry on. The slip of paper helps me keep my place, but… sometimes I’ve got the right line and still need to remind myself what it’s about.

interview.interviewer: What kinds of treatment or support are part of your week?
interview.patient: I take a prescribed tablet in the evening, and I work with someone at the clinic on ways to manage distractions. Things like the slip of paper I mentioned—we’ve been practising ways to make the reading easier to stay with.

interview.interviewer: How are you getting on with assignments at home and with time spent in class?
interview.patient:
At home, I’m still leaving some of the reading too late. I like the course, so it’s frustrating… I want to get more done before I set off.

In class, if several things are going on, I can lose the thread and find it hard to get back into what’s being said. It’s not so much voices interrupting now—that hasn’t happened in the last few classes.

interview.interviewer: What gets in the way there?
interview.patient: “In class, you mean? When several things are happening, my attention gets pulled away from what’s being said. Then… I’m trying to catch up with the bit I missed, and I lose the next bit too.”

interview.interviewer: I was asking about class itself. What has it been like to concentrate during the last few classes?
interview.patient: It’s still been hard to follow when several things are happening at once. I miss a bit, then… while I’m trying to work out what I missed, the class has moved on. That’s been the difficulty in the last few classes, rather than voices interrupting.

interview.interviewer: Have you heard anything unexpected, such as a voice when nobody is speaking, in the past month or so?
interview.patient: About a month ago, at home, I heard a voice say a single name when nobody was speaking. Just that… I haven’t noticed it since.

interview.interviewer: Returning to reading, where do you find it easiest to finish a passage?
interview.patient: In the library, where it’s quiet. If people are talking nearby, I lose my place more easily… without that, it’s easier to stay with the passage and finish it.

interview.interviewer: How would you like to arrange your study time next week?
interview.patient: I’d like to set aside some time in the library before Tuesday evening, rather than leave it for the trip to class. Maybe do a short passage at a time… use the slip of paper again, since that helped last week.

item1.A: With a slip of paper marking the line, the patient finished the short passage last week.
item1.B: With a slip of paper marking the line, the patient left the short passage unfinished last week.

item2.A: The patient finds a piece of reading easier to resume than a hands-on task.
item2.B: The patient finds a hands-on task easier to resume than a piece of reading.
